title: time-weighted-burn-rate-smoothing-experiments
content:
Executive summary:

This note documents an experimental approach for smoothing Redwood's revenue/commit burn and customer per-GPU economics across time using a time-weighted amortization mechanism. The goal is to reduce month-to-month revenue volatility from large reserved GPU pool commits, make unit economics more predictable for customers, and create incentives for steady utilization without creating unacceptable under-recovery risk for Redwood.

Problem statement / motivation:
- Large reserved commitments (multi-month/annual) create lumpy cash flows and sharp changes in utilization metrics when customers onboard or churn.
- Current per-month recognition can overstate near-term utilization and artificially inflate reported efficiency metrics in ramp months, then drop in later months.
- Product and finance need a lightweight mechanism to: (1) smooth revenue recognition for planning/forecasting, (2) show customers a stable effective per-GPU-hour price that rewards steady usage, and (3) preserve upside on burstable usage.

Proposed mechanism (time-weighted burn-rate smoothing):
1) Amortize committed pool cost across a configurable smoothing window (W months) rather than the full invoice month when payment happens.
2) Create a rolling credit/debit ledger per customer pool: when a commit is executed, a time-weighted credit schedule is added (e.g., 30% of commit cost applied to month0, 20% to month1, etc.), configurable shapes supported (flat, front-loaded, back-loaded, exponential decay).
3) During each month, compute an "effective committed unit cost" per GPU-hour as: amortized_commit_contrib / (actual_hours_consumed + floor_hours_buffer). If customer consumes less than the smoothing-window expected hours, the remaining amortized portion stays in the ledger and continues to amortize over remaining months.
4) Bursts above committed capacity are billed at on-demand margin on top of the amortized committed unit cost; bursts do not reduce amortized schedule but may generate separate credits if they convert to longer commits.

Why time-weighted vs simple monthly amortization:
- Time-weighted shapes allow us to test customer-friendly recognition (front-loaded discounts for quick adoption) or revenue-protecting back-loaded shapes depending on segment and risk appetite.
- Smoothing windows reduce month-to-month surprise in top-line planning and provide clearer signals for capacity provisioning.

Spreadsheet layout (reference workbook: sheet:1w2X-example-time-weighted):
- Inputs sheet: customer_id, pool_size_gpus, commit_amount_usd, commit_term_months, smoothing_window_months, amort_shape (flat|front|back|decay), expected_utilization_pct, buffer_hours_per_gpu_per_month, on_demand_markup_pct, churn_risk_pct_per_month
- Schedule sheet: per-month amortized USD amount (vector length = smoothing_window_months), remaining_unamortized_usd, cumulative_recognized_usd
- Utilization sheet: actual_gpu_hours_by_month, effective_committed_gpu_hours, burst_gpu_hours, effective_unit_price_usd_per_gpu_hour (amortized + markup where applicable)
- Scenarios sheet: compare W = {3,6,12} months, amort_shapes = {flat, front-60/30/10, decay-0.5}, churn buckets = {low, medium, high}

Key formulas (plain text so you can copy into sheets):
- total_hours_in_month = pool_size_gpus * hours_per_gpu_per_month (use 730 as base)
- amortized_per_month[i] = commit_amount_usd * shape_weight[i] for i in 0..W-1 (shape weights sum to 1)
- effective_committed_unit_cost = amortized_per_month_this_month / (max(actual_gpu_hours, expected_committed_hours * utilization_pct) + buffer_hours)
- effective_customer_price_for_month = effective_committed_unit_cost for usage within committed hours; for burst_hours: burst_price = on_demand_unit_cost * (1 + on_demand_markup_pct)

Illustrative worked example (numbers):
- Customer A: commits $144,000 for 8 GPUs for 12 months (invoice paid month0). Base hours/month = 8 * 730 = 5,840 h.
- Scenario 1 (W=12, flat): amortized_per_month = 144,000 / 12 = 12,000 USD/month. If actual consumption month1 = 4,000h, effective_committed_unit_cost = 12,000 / 4,000 = 3.00 USD / GPU-hour. If month2 ramps to 5,500h, cost = 12,000 / 5,500 = 2.18 USD/h.
- Scenario 2 (W=6, front-loaded 50/30/20 remainder): amortized_month0 = 72,000, month1 = 43,200, month2 = 28,800, then zero afterwards. Month0 effective unit cost for 4,000h = 72,000/4,000 = 18 USD/h — shows the danger of aggressive front-loading without buffer.

Observations from quick sensitivity runs (spreadsheet):
- Short W (3 months) with front-loading reduces early perceived price for customer (if front-loaded as negative credit) but massively increases Redwood exposure if utilization doesn't materialize.
- Longer W (12 months) smooths both customer and Redwood P&L; it also aligns with fiscal forecasting and reduces churn signal noise in product metrics.
- Buffer hours (floor_hours) materially reduce volatility of per-hour prices in early months; introducing a small buffer (10-20% of expected committed hours) keeps effective price within reasonable bounds while preserving incentives.

Experiment matrix (to run in sheets):
- Axis A: smoothing_window = [3,6,12]
- Axis B: amort_shape = [flat, front(60/30/10), back(10/30/60), decay(half-life=3m)]
- Axis C: expected_utilization = [40%, 60%, 80%, 100%]
- Axis D: churn_risk = [0%, 2%, 5% / month]
- For each combination compute: recognized_revenue_over_12m, tail_exposure (unamortized USD after 12m), average_effective_price_per_gpu_hour, revenue_variance_monthly

Go-to-market / product implications and rollout suggestions:
- Start with an internal pilot for new mid-market Reserved pools only; keep smoothing_window = 12 months and flat amort_shape for first 90 days. Monitor key metrics: recognized_revenue variance, collection deltas, net churn, conversion_to_reserved_after_burst.
- Offer customers an 'Economy Smoothing' badge: display their effective price band in the Console with an explanation of the smoothing window. Keep default conservative so finance is comfortable.
- Build a "Smoothing Simulator" in the Console bill preview: allow customers to try W and shapes and show impact on monthly invoice and effective per-hour price.
- For high-trust enterprise accounts, allow negotiated amort_shape and shorter W with additional credit protections (security deposit, early-termination fee schedule).

Metrics to track (dashboards to add in Console/Finance reporting):
- monthly_recognized_amortized_revenue_by_customer_pool
- amortization_ledger_balance (per pool) and tail_exposure
- effective_price_percentile_by_cohort (p50/p90)
- churn_vs_amort_shape_cohort
- capacity_planning_signal_adjusted (smoothed utilization used for capacity provisioning decisions)

Risks and mitigations:
- Under-recovery risk if customers underutilize for long periods: mitigate by conservative buffer, minimum monthly floor billing, or financial hold back (deposit).
- Accounting treatment: engage finance to validate recognition approach (this is a modeling worksheet for product/ops — any final proposal must be vetted by FP&A and accounting).
- Customer confusion: require clear in-console explanations and billing previews. Show historical effective price bands so customers understand the smoothing behavior.

Next steps / action items:
- Product: wire up the Smoothing Simulator mock in Console prototype (owner: Priya, ETA: 3 weeks).
- Finance: validate recognition model and sample journal entries for W=12 flat (owner: Evan, ETA: 2 weeks).
- Analytics/Infra: add amortization_ledger to billing schema and expose daily_balance for pilot customers (owner: Luca, ETA: 6 weeks).
- Sales/CS: draft one-pager for mid-market pilot offers and guardrails (owner: Marisol, ETA: 1 week).

Appendix: checklist for spreadsheet sanity checks:
- Verify shape weights sum to 1.0 for each amort_shape.
- Test corner cases: zero consumption months, full-churn at month1, mid-term increase to committed pool size.
- Run stochastics: sample churn paths (Monte Carlo) to see distribution of tail_exposure under each amort_shape.
- Confirm hours_per_month constant is consistent (730 vs 720) across all sheets.

Notes to reviewers: this is an exploratory draft intended for internal review. The attached spreadsheet (sheet:1w2X-example-time-weighted) contains the runnable scenarios described above. Feedback especially requested on: recommended default W for self-serve vs enterprise, acceptable buffer percent, and sample journal treatment assumptions for finance.
